items.title: Paint: Accurate, efficient, and sparse Model Inversion via peripheral sparsification and anchor alignment
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (verified on article pages; occasional CC0)
items.abstract: by Jaehyeon Choi, Minjun Kim, U Kang How can we reconstruct training data from a pre-trained model without access to the original dataset? Model Inversion (MI) attempts to synthesize samples similar to the training dataset. This capability is particularly useful in data-free applications, such as data-free quantization and data-free knowledge transfer, where synthetic data replace inaccessible training samples. For these applications, MI needs to generate high-fidelity samples to preserve semantic information while remaining computationally efficient, enabling scalable generation for reliable downstream performance. However, existing MI methods fail to achieve both high fidelity and efficiency simultaneously. In this paper, we propose Paint (Peripheral sparsification and Anchor-aligned INversion Technique), an accurate, efficient, and sparse MI framework for generating high-fidelity synthetic data. Paint integrates low-pass filtering during inversion to suppress high-frequency noise, aligns salient regions toward anchor with peripheral sparsification to preserve object structures during sparse inversion, and exploits soft targets to better capture the predictive uncertainty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Paint improves inversion efficiency for ViTs and achieves accuracy gains of up to 5.33%p in data-free scenarios.

items.title: A generic route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: We propose a generic autonomous route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations through nonlinear feedback from a finite-rate charging variable. Near the threshold of an oscillatory ion-acoustic instability, a multiple-scale reduction yields a Stuart-Landau amplitude equation, represented by a van der Pol-type modal surrogate and coupled to debris-charge evolution in a prototype case of plasma-debris interaction scenario. For a debris-induced ion-ion counter-streaming instability, charge-dependent forcing and frequency modulation, finite charging relaxation, phase-lagged modal response, mixed nonlinear feedback, and saturation form a closed dynamical system without an externally imposed periodic driver. Numerical bifurcation and Lyapunov analyses reveal multistability and a bounded chaotic branch reached through period doubling bifurcation and band formation. We test the proposed mechanism using a one-dimensional open-boundary \emph{hybrid} particle-in-cell-Monte Carlo collision simulation incorporating particle collection, photoemission, secondary-electron emission, and surface regulation. Weak-form sparse regression identifies finite intervals whose projected dynamics reproduce the sign structure of the reduced model, while independent $0$-$1$ chaos test, nonlinear predicatbility, surrogate-data, and Lyapunov diagnostics provide localized evidence of deterministic chaotic organization in the subsonic case. The combined results establish a proof-of-principle route by which a self-excited plasma mode can become chaotic through internally generated charging feedback.

items.title: Deciphering multiple binding modes in large protein complexes via Enhanced Sampling and beta-VAE: the CYFIP1-eIF4E case
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) drives cap-dependent translation, regulated by 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) competing for its dorsal and lateral surfaces. CYFIP1, a scaffold protein, is both a WAVE Regulatory Complex component and a non-canonical 4E-BP repressing translation via a short helical motif, linked to autism spectrum disorders and cancer. Prior work modeled only this isolated motif as a peptide, leaving the full interface uncharacterized. Starting from this preliminary evidence, we modeled the full-length proteins as flexible partners: all-atom simulations fed a data-driven docking search (HADDOCK3), which guided funnel-restrained Temperature-Accelerated Molecular Dynamics of a coarse-grained Martini 3 representation. Ten replicas accumulated 100 $μ$s of enhanced sampling. Funnel-restraint variables efficiently sample binding and unbinding but are structurally degenerate: direct clustering of the raw trajectory collapses these poses into poorly resolved groups. We instead reweighted the biased trajectories onto a contact-based latent space built by benchmarking PCA against a beta-Variational Autoencoder, then clustered minima of the equilibrium free-energy surface: only intermediate regularization resolved distinct, homogeneous modes. Three such modes recur, engaging eIF4E's canonical dorsal site, its non-canonical lateral site, and both. We find that CYFIP1 also engages eIF4E through a second surface, the same that mediates its WAVE-complex dimerization, and a basic patch. Both plausibly explain residual binding previously reported after motif mutation. This suggests its translational and cytoskeletal roles compete for the same surface. Most contacts on eIF4E fall outside this dorsal/lateral interface. This heterogeneous, plastic ensemble offers a structural basis for mutagenesis and therapeutic peptide design.

items.title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Artoghrul Alishbayli, Karol Przewrocki, Paul van Heumen, Bernhard Englitz Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

items.title: ST-FateFlow: Continuous Gene-Spatial Reconstruction with Differentiation-Potential Learning from Time-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Time-resolved spatial transcriptomics provides a powerful view of dynamic biological processes by measuring cellular states together with their spatial organization across time. However, destructive profiling and experimental cost restrict observations to a few discrete time points collected from independent samples, with no known cell pairing across time. This makes it difficult to reconstruct gene expression and tissue organization at unobserved stages and to characterize differentiation-associated dynamics. Here, we introduce ST-FateFlow, a flow-matching framework for continuous gene-spatial dynamics and differentiation-potential learning. ST-FateFlow jointly learns gene-expression and spatial-coordinate velocity fields, enabling interpolation of missing time points and continuous modeling of transcriptional evolution and tissue remodeling. In parallel, it independently learns a time-conditioned differentiation potential, whose values organize cell states along inferred differentiation progressions and support the analysis of differentiation-associated transcriptional changes. Across multiple time-resolved spatial transcriptomics datasets, ST-FateFlow effectively captures coordinated gene-expression and spatial dynamics. Case studies further show that the learned potential landscapes are consistent with known developmental and regenerative trajectories and help identify candidate genes associated with differentiation progression.

items.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency ( f ) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/ f 4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. items.title: Adaptation of an herbivorous arthropod to green tea plants by overcoming catechin defenses
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Green tea catechins protect tea plants from biotic stressors. Among herbivorous mites, the generalist Tetranychus urticae has not been reported as a tea pest. In contrast, some populations of Tetranychus kanzawai thrive on tea plants. Here, we investigated the mechanism of this adaptation. Green tea catechins were repellent and toxic to T. urticae and tea non-adapted T. kanzawai and had an antifeedant effect on the latter. We identified an intradiol ring-cleavage dioxygenase DOG15 , a gene horizontally transferred from fungi, as required for the adaptation of T. kanzawai to tea plants. Tea feeding strongly induces DOG15 expression in tea-adapted T. kanzawai , with mRNA and protein levels up to 31.6 and 12.1 times higher than in tea-fed T. urticae . We also identified two amino acid substitutions in DOG15 between the two Tetranychus species that increased the catechin-cleaving activity of the T. kanzawai enzyme. These substitutions predispose T. kanzawai but not T. urticae for the adaptation to tea plants. Inducible expression of modified DOG15 then enables T. kanzawai to efficiently detoxify green tea catechins. Our findings reveal how a horizontally transferred gene can be co-opted through structural and regulatory changes to overcome plant chemical defenses.

items.title: WNK-SPAK/OSR1 signaling pathway facilitates ictal activity via reduced neuronal chloride extrusion rate
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Seizures upregulate Na + -K + –2Cl − (NKCC1)-mediated Cl − influx and downregulate K + -Cl − (KCC2)-mediated Cl − efflux via the WNK-SPAK/OSR1 kinases, leading to cytoplasmic chloride ([Cl − ] i ) accumulation, reduced GABAergic inhibition, and anticonvulsant failure. Early studies found that inhibiting WNK-kinase reduced baseline [Cl − ] i (E Cl ) and seizures via increased KCC2 activity. However, increased KCC2 activity alone should not affect E Cl , whose determinants are more complex. We determined the net effects of the WNK-SPAK/OSR1 pathway inhibitor WNK463 on E Cl and [Cl − ] i transients during spontaneous ictal-like discharges (ILDs) in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures from mice. We found that WNK463 reduced interictal [Cl − ] i , but did not change baseline [Cl − ] i measured in the presence of TTX. WNK463 enhanced neuronal Cl − extrusion during and after ILDs before abolishing ILDs. Pharmacological inhibition and targeted siRNA silencing demonstrated that the anti-ictal effects of WNK463 involved both NKCC1 and KCC2. Our data support a mechanism whereby mutual NKCC1 inhibition and KCC2 activation via the WNK-SPAK/OSR1 pathway exert powerful anti-ictal effects by facilitating [Cl − ] i extrusion during ILDs.

items.title: ITK deficiency protects against autoimmune pulmonary hemorrhage in mice by promoting amphiregulin-producing regulatory T cells
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Pulmonary hemorrhage (PH) is a life-threatening manifestation of systemic autoimmunity caused by immune-mediated disruption of the alveolar capillary barrier. Despite high mortality, the molecular checkpoints that shift destructive inflammation toward protective immune regulation remain poorly defined. Here, using a pristane-induced PH mouse model, we identify interleukin-2-inducible T-cell kinase (ITK) as a critical regulator of autoimmune lung injury. ITK deficiency ( Itk⁻ / ⁻ ) conferred near-complete protection from PH and associated multiorgan injury, accompanied by reduced proinflammatory monocytes and neutrophils and increased Foxp3 + regulatory T cells (Tregs). Adoptive transfer of Itk⁻ / ⁻ Tregs protected wild-type recipients from PH and suppressed systemic proinflammatory cytokines, identifying Tregs as key mediators of tissue protection. Mechanistically, lung Itk ⁻ / ⁻ Tregs exhibited increased amphiregulin, a mediator of tissue repair. Transcriptomic profiling further showed that ITK loss reprogrammed Tregs toward a metabolically and functionally enhanced state, with enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, mTORC1, and STAT5 signaling, and tissue-repair programs. These findings establish ITK as a regulator of the balance between pulmonary injury and reparative immunity and support targeting the ITK axis in severe inflammatory lung disease.

items.title: Neuronal XOR computation requires temporally activated synaptic information
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Yanheng Li, Xiaojuan Sun, Yunliang Zang Single neurons can perform complex exclusive-or (XOR) computation which is conventionally thought to need multilayer networks, yet the biophysical mechanisms and the robustness of such computations under stochastic synaptic drive remain unclear. Using biologically realistic modeling, we demonstrate that dendritic depolarization block provides a universal and robust mechanism for XOR-like computation. Voltage-gated calcium channels enable a non-monotonic input-output relationship: moderate asynchronous drive evokes spiking, whereas excessive drive induces a sustained plateau that suppresses output, naturally implementing XOR logic computation. This computation is strictly gated by temporal distribution of synaptic inputs rather than spatial distribution; the XOR-like response is robust across diverse dendritic configurations but collapses under synchronous activation. Dendritic depolarization block propagates to the soma via dendrite-soma coupling, establishing a neuronal output-limiting mechanism. The computation is highly efficient, leveraging a frequency–synapse-count trade-off to ensure stable logic operations across varying levels of background activity. Cross-morphological validation confirms that XOR-like computation is morphology-independent, representing a generalizable biophysical principle of neural information processing.

items.title: An Exploration of Physical and Chemical Representation in Coarse-Grained, Machine-Learned Protein Models
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Machine-learned coarse-graining has emerged as a reliable framework for building protein models that accurately and efficiently sample their relevant conformational landscape. Existing studies assume a predefined map from full- to coarse-grained resolution. However, the choice of map strongly affects the quality of the models. Here, we study the dependence of system-specific machine-learned coarse-grained (MLCG) models across 7 mapping choices, spanning different resolutions and embedding types for coarse-grained beads. We show that resolution and chemical diversity do not always correlate with accuracy, and that accurate protein-specific models can be generated using minimal chemical diversity if the latent space representation of the system has high enough dimensionality.

items.title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Pablo Sanchez-Martin, Irene Elices, Alicia Garrido-Peña, Carlos Garcia-Saura, Rafael Levi, Francisco B. Rodriguez, Pablo Varona In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles. Our results help understand the mechanisms underlying the autonomous cycle-by-cycle sequential coordination and the relationships between intervals from consecutive cycles when a slow modulatory action establishes a common trend across the rhythm.

items.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Sebastian Manuel Geli, Juan Manuel Monti, Adrián Ponce-Alvarez, Gustavo Deco, Yonatan Sanz Perl A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region’s future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation–dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain’s memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.
